questions.prompt: A biological investigation produces a clear trend but substantial scatter. (a) Distinguish accuracy from precision. (2) (b) Explain how increasing sample size can improve confidence in a conclusion. (2) (c) State two reasons why correlation alone does not prove causation. (2)
hints: Define the two measurement terms separately.
Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: Define the two measurement terms separately.
Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype is 0.36. (a) Calculate the recessive allele frequency $q$. (2) (b) Calculate the expected heterozygote frequency. (2) (c) State two assumptions of the Hardy–Weinberg model. (2)
hints: The recessive phenotype frequency is $q^2$.
Use $p+q=1$ and $p^2+2pq+q^2=1$.
questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.36$, so $q=0.60$. (b) $p=1-q=0.40$ and $2pq=0.480$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype is 0.49. (a) Calculate the recessive allele frequency $q$. (2) (b) Calculate the expected heterozygote frequency. (2) (c) State two assumptions of the Hardy–Weinberg model. (2)
hints: The recessive phenotype frequency is $q^2$.
Use $p+q=1$ and $p^2+2pq+q^2=1$.
questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.49$, so $q=0.70$. (b) $p=1-q=0.30$ and $2pq=0.420$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

Use $p+q=1$ and $p^2+2pq+q^2=1$.
questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.64$, so $q=0.80$. (b) $p=1-q=0.20$ and $2pq=0.320$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A population becomes geographically isolated. (a) Explain how isolation can lead to speciation. (5) (b) Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies. (3) (c) State one method used to estimate abundance of an immobile species. (1)
hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.
questions.solution: (a) Isolation prevents gene flow; different mutations/selection pressures and genetic drift cause allele-frequency divergence; reproductive isolation eventually develops. (b) Individuals with advantageous heritable alleles have greater reproductive success, so those alleles increase in frequency. (c) Quadrat sampling. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.
questions.solution: (a) Isolation prevents gene flow; different mutations/selection pressures and genetic drift cause allele-frequency divergence; reproductive isolation eventually develops. (b) Individuals with advantageous heritable alleles have greater reproductive success, so those alleles increase in frequency. (c) Quadrat sampling. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A population becomes geographically isolated. (a) Explain how isolation can lead to speciation. (5) (b) Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies. (3) (c) State one method used to estimate abundance of an immobile species. (1)
hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.
questions.solution: (a) Isolation prevents gene flow; different mutations/selection pressures and genetic drift cause allele-frequency divergence; reproductive isolation eventually develops. (b) Individuals with advantageous heritable alleles have greater reproductive success, so those alleles increase in frequency. (c) Quadrat sampling. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A pathogen enters the body for the first time. (a) Describe the primary immune response involving B lymphocytes. (5) (b) Explain why a second exposure usually produces a faster response. (2) (c) Explain one way vaccination can reduce spread through a population. (2)
hints: Use clonal selection and expansion.
Memory cells explain the secondary response.
questions.solution: (a) A specific B cell is activated by antigen/helper T-cell signalling, undergoes clonal expansion, and differentiates into plasma cells producing specific antibody and memory cells. (b) Memory cells are already present and rapidly form plasma cells. (c) More immune individuals reduce transmission chains and the effective reproduction of the pathogen. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A pathogen enters the body for the first time. (a) Describe the primary immune response involving B lymphocytes. (5) (b) Explain why a second exposure usually produces a faster response. (2) (c) Explain one way vaccination can reduce spread through a population. (2)
hints: Use clonal selection and expansion.
Memory cells explain the secondary response.
questions.solution: (a) A specific B cell is activated by antigen/helper T-cell signalling, undergoes clonal expansion, and differentiates into plasma cells producing specific antibody and memory cells. (b) Memory cells are already present and rapidly form plasma cells. (c) More immune individuals reduce transmission chains and the effective reproduction of the pathogen. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A biological investigation produces a clear trend but substantial scatter. (a) Distinguish accuracy from precision. (2) (b) Explain how increasing sample size can improve confidence in a conclusion. (2) (c) State two reasons why correlation alone does not prove causation. (2)
hints: Define the two measurement terms separately.
Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: Define the two measurement terms separately.
Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A biological investigation produces a clear trend but substantial scatter. (a) Distinguish accuracy from precision. (2) (b) Explain how increasing sample size can improve confidence in a conclusion. (2) (c) State two reasons why correlation alone does not prove causation. (2)
hints: Define the two measurement terms separately.
Think about confounding variables.
questions.solution: (a) Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values to each other. (b) A larger sample reduces the influence of random sampling variation and gives a more representative estimate. (c) A third variable may affect both variables, and the direction of causation may be uncertain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. (a) Describe how the pancreas detects and responds to this change. (4) (b) Explain two effects of insulin that lower blood glucose. (4) (c) Explain why this is an example of negative feedback. (2)
hints: Identify the receptor/control tissue and hormone.
Negative feedback reverses a deviation.
questions.solution: (a) Beta cells detect increased glucose and secrete insulin. (b) Insulin increases glucose uptake by responsive cells and stimulates glycogenesis/greater glucose use, lowering blood glucose. (c) The response opposes the original change and moves the controlled variable back towards its set point. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: Two groups of organisms have sample sizes 12 and 12, with mean values 24.2 and 20.1. (a) State a suitable statistical test for comparing the means of two independent groups when the data are approximately normally distributed. (1) (b) Explain what a p-value below 0.05 means. (2) (c) Give two improvements to the experimental design. (2)
hints: Match the test to two independent means.
A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: (a) Independent-samples t-test. (b) If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining a difference at least this extreme is below 5%; the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. (c) e.g. increase sample size, randomise allocation/sampling, control confounding variables, repeat measurements. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]

questions.prompt: Two groups of organisms have sample sizes 15 and 15, with mean values 23.8 and 21.0. (a) State a suitable statistical test for comparing the means of two independent groups when the data are approximately normally distributed. (1) (b) Explain what a p-value below 0.05 means. (2) (c) Give two improvements to the experimental design. (2)
hints: Match the test to two independent means.
A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: (a) Independent-samples t-test. (b) If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining a difference at least this extreme is below 5%; the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. (c) e.g. increase sample size, randomise allocation/sampling, control confounding variables, repeat measurements. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]

questions.prompt: Two groups of organisms have sample sizes 12 and 12, with mean values 24.2 and 20.1. (a) State a suitable statistical test for comparing the means of two independent groups when the data are approximately normally distributed. (1) (b) Explain what a p-value below 0.05 means. (2) (c) Give two improvements to the experimental design. (2)
hints: Match the test to two independent means.
A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: (a) Independent-samples t-test. (b) If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining a difference at least this extreme is below 5%; the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. (c) e.g. increase sample size, randomise allocation/sampling, control confounding variables, repeat measurements. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]
